---
title: "The simulation"
subtitle: "`src/simulation.ts`: the model on the Rapier physics engine"
---

This chapter is the heart of the program. The `Simulation` class owns a Rapier world in which every
cell is a rigid body with a capsule-shaped collider. On every step Rapier moves the bodies and
resolves their contacts; then, on growth steps, the model makes cells grow, divide, leave the
chamber or die, and attaches cells near the side walls to the surface. Every `snapshotInterval`
steps it records the state of the colony.

The class uses no browser or Node.js APIs, so the same code runs in the
[command-line runner](cli.qmd) and in the [browser](browser.qmd). Using it takes three lines:

```ts
const sim = await Simulation.create({ seed: 7 });
while (sim.stepCount < 3000) { sim.step(); }
sim.states.toPieces();
```

## Overview

The file defines two records, one for cells and one for anchors, and the class itself:

```{.typescript file=src/simulation.ts}
<<sim-imports>>

<<sim-rapier-init>>

<<sim-cell-record>>

<<sim-anchor-record>>

<<sim-wall-thickness>>

export class Simulation {
  <<sim-fields>>

  <<sim-create>>

  <<sim-constructor>>

  <<sim-public-api>>

  <<sim-step>>

  <<sim-create-world>>

  <<sim-rebuild-world>>

  <<sim-remove-marked-cells>>

  <<sim-remove-anchors>>

  <<sim-damping>>

  <<sim-over-stretched>>

  <<sim-grow-divide-mark>>

  <<sim-take-snapshot>>

  <<sim-create-cell>>

  <<sim-collider-desc>>

  <<sim-resize-collider>>

  <<sim-reset-cell>>

  <<sim-create-anchor>>

  <<sim-detach-anchors>>

  <<sim-create-walls>>
}
```

One call to `step()` does the following:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["<b>Physics</b><br/>Rapier moves the bodies<br/>and resolves contacts"] --> B["<b>Growth</b><br/>if it is a group's turn:<br/>grow, divide, exit, die,<br/>anchor; remove marked cells"]
  B --> C["<b>Anchors</b><br/>once per cycle:<br/>release expired and<br/>over-stretched ones"]
  C --> D["<b>Rebuild</b><br/>every 10 000 steps:<br/>fresh Rapier world"]
  D --> E["<b>Snapshot</b><br/>every 300 steps:<br/>record all cells"]
```

## Loading Rapier

Rapier is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. The npm package
`@dimforge/rapier2d-simd-compat` is the build that uses WebAssembly's SIMD instructions (about
twice as fast as the plain build here) with the WebAssembly module inlined in the JavaScript file,
so it loads the same way in Node.js and in the browser, without a separate `.wasm` file.

```{.typescript #sim-imports}
import RAPIER from "@dimforge/rapier2d-simd-compat";
import type { Collider, ColliderDesc, ImpulseJoint, RigidBody, World } from "@dimforge/rapier2d-simd-compat";
import {
  CHAMBER, COLOR_CENTRE, COLOR_INITIAL, COLOR_WALL, DEFAULT_PARAMS, Point, RGB,
  SimulationParams, cellMassProperties, checkParams, continuousDampingRate, dragFraction, orientationOf,
} from "./model.js";
import { Rng, mulberry32, randomSeed } from "./rng.js";
import { CellState, StateRecorder } from "./states.js";
```

The WebAssembly module has to be instantiated before any Rapier object is created. `initRapier`
does that once and hands every later caller the same promise. `rapierVersion` reports the version
in use; the runner prints it at the start of a run, since results depend on it.

```{.typescript #sim-rapier-init}
let initialised: Promise<void> | null = null;

export function initRapier(): Promise<void> {
  if (!initialised) { initialised = RAPIER.init(); }
  return initialised;
}

export function rapierVersion(): string {
  return RAPIER.version();
}
```

## The state of the simulation

### Cells

Each cell is a record that ties the model's view of the cell to its Rapier objects:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | the cell's identity in the recorded states; never reused |
| `body`, `collider` | the Rapier rigid body and its capsule collider |
| `sqrtFriction` | the square root of the cell's friction coefficient (see [Creating a cell](#creating-a-cell)) |
| `flipped` | whether the collider is turned by π on its body (only with `refreshContacts` = 2) |
| `mass`, `inertia` | fixed at birth |
| `length` | distance between the centres of the two end caps |
| `growthRate` | the factor by which the length grows on each growth event |
| `phase` | the cell's growth group; daughters inherit it |
| `reproductiveLength` | the length at which the cell divides |
| `color` | the cell's region colour |
| `anchors` | the anchors currently holding this cell |
| `removed` | marked for removal (it left the chamber or died) |

```{.typescript #sim-cell-record}
interface Cell {
  id: number;
  body: RigidBody;
  collider: Collider;
  sqrtFriction: number;
  flipped: boolean;
  mass: number;
  inertia: number;
  length: number;
  growthRate: number;
  phase: number;
  reproductiveLength: number;
  color: RGB;
  anchors: Anchor[];
  removed: boolean;
}
```

### Anchors

An anchor is a fixed Rapier body at the point where a cell attached, plus a spring joint between
that body and the cell. It remembers the step at which it was made (anchors expire), and its spring
constants, so that the spring can be recreated when the world is rebuilt. `cell` and `joint` become
`null` when the cell divides or is removed: the anchor point stays until it expires, but holds
nothing.

```{.typescript #sim-anchor-record}
interface Anchor {
  body: RigidBody;
  x: number;
  y: number;
  createdAtStep: number;
  cell: Cell | null;
  joint: ImpulseJoint | null;
  stiffness: number;
  damping: number;
}
```

### The simulation's own fields

```{.typescript #sim-wall-thickness}
const WALL_THICKNESS = 2;
```

The public fields are the run's parameters (the defaults with the overrides applied, plus the
seed), the Rapier world, the recorded states and the step counter. The world is replaced every
`rebuildInterval` steps, so callers should not keep a reference to it. The private fields are the
random number generator, the next free cell id, the live cells and anchors, and a reusable zero
vector for Rapier calls.

```{.typescript #sim-fields}
public readonly params: SimulationParams;
public world: World;
public readonly states: StateRecorder = new StateRecorder();
public stepCount: number = 0;

private readonly rng: Rng;
private nextId: number = 1;
private cells: Cell[] = [];
private anchors: Anchor[] = [];
private readonly zero = { x: 0, y: 0 };
```

## Creating a simulation

`Simulation.create` is the way in: it loads Rapier (once) and builds a simulation. Any parameter
not given takes its default from `DEFAULT_PARAMS`; without a seed, a random one is drawn (and
reported in `params.seed`, so the run can be repeated).

```{.typescript #sim-create}
public static async create(overrides: Partial<SimulationParams> = {}): Promise<Simulation> {
  await initRapier();
  return new Simulation(overrides);
}
```

The constructor checks the parameters, seeds the random number generator and creates the world.
Then it scatters the initial cells over the chamber: a random position, angle and length each,
drawn in that order (the order matters: the same seed must give the same colony). The initial cells
are dealt into the growth groups in turn. The walls come last, as in the testbed.

```{.typescript #sim-constructor}
constructor(overrides: Partial<SimulationParams> = {}) {
  this.params = { ...DEFAULT_PARAMS, seed: randomSeed(), ...overrides };
  const p = this.params;
  checkParams(p);
  this.rng = mulberry32(p.seed);
  this.world = this.createWorld();

  for (let i = 0; i < p.initialCells; ++i) {
    const x = this.rng() * (p.maxX - p.minX) + p.minX;
    const y = this.rng() * (p.maxY - p.minY) + p.minY;
    const angle = this.rng() * 2 * Math.PI;
    const size = 0.2 * this.rng() * (p.maxSize - p.minSize) + p.minSize;
    this.cells.push(this.createCell(x, y, angle, size, COLOR_INITIAL, 0, i % p.growthGroups));
  }
  this.createWalls();
}
```

## Reading the state

The rest of the program sees the cells only through three members. `forEachCell` reports each
cell's centre, angle, length, colour and id at full precision; the [overlap check](overlap.qmd)
and the [drawing](rendering.qmd) use it. `forEachAnchor` reports each anchor point together with
the centre of the cell it holds, or `null` if it holds nothing. Callbacks avoid building arrays of
objects on every frame.

```{.typescript #sim-public-api}
public get cellCount(): number {
  return this.cells.length;
}

public forEachCell(fn: (x: number, y: number, angle: number, length: number, color: RGB, id: number) => void): void {
  for (const cell of this.cells) {
    const t = cell.body.translation();
    fn(t.x, t.y, cell.body.rotation(), cell.length, cell.color, cell.id);
  }
}

public forEachAnchor(fn: (x: number, y: number, cell: Point | null) => void): void {
  for (const anchor of this.anchors) {
    fn(anchor.x, anchor.y, anchor.cell ? anchor.cell.body.translation() : null);
  }
}
```

## One step

`step()` advances the simulation by $1/\text{hertz}$ and returns whether it recorded a snapshot.
First Rapier advances the world. Then the step's position in the growth cycle,
$\text{offset} = \text{stepCount} \bmod G$, decides what else happens. With $G = 25$ and 5 groups,
the groups' slots are 5 steps apart: group 0 grows when the offset is 0, group 1 when it is 5, and
so on. Removing cells is only needed when some were marked. Anchors are checked once per cycle, at
offset 0. With the collider-replacement fix (`refreshContacts` = 1), the world is rebuilt every
`rebuildInterval` steps, for the reason explained in [Growing a collider](#growing-a-collider).

```{.typescript #sim-step}
public step(): boolean {
  const p = this.params;
  for (let i = 0; i < p.substeps; i++) { this.world.step(); }
  this.stepCount += 1;
  const offset = this.stepCount % p.growthInterval;
  const spacing = p.growthInterval / p.growthGroups;

  if (offset % spacing === 0 && this.growDivideAndMark(offset / spacing)) { this.removeMarkedCells(); }

  if (offset === 0) { this.removeAnchors(); }

  if (p.refreshContacts === 1 && p.rebuildInterval > 0 && this.stepCount % p.rebuildInterval === 0) {
    this.rebuildWorld();
  }

  if (this.stepCount % p.snapshotInterval === 0) {
    this.takeSnapshot();
    return true;
  }
  return false;
}
```

## The Rapier world

The world has no gravity: the chamber is seen from above, and the cells lie flat in it. The time
step and the solver settings come from the [parameters](model.qmd#time-stepping-and-the-solver).
The contact stiffness is set through Rapier's *contact natural frequency*: the stiffer the
contacts, the less cells sink into each other under pressure.

```{.typescript #sim-create-world}
private createWorld(): World {
  const p = this.params;
  const world = new RAPIER.World({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  world.timestep = 1 / (p.hertz * p.substeps);
  world.numSolverIterations = p.solverIterations;
  world.numInternalPgsIterations = p.pgsIterations;
  if (p.contactFrequency > 0) {
    world.integrationParameters.contact_natural_frequency = p.contactFrequency;
  }
  return world;
}
```

### The chamber walls

All walls are colliders on one fixed body. The testbed's walls were zero-thickness edges; here the
side and top walls are boxes 2 units thick whose inner faces lie exactly on those edges, because a
packed colony can push a cell through an infinitely thin wall but not through a thick one. For a
vertical edge the box extends outwards, away from the chamber; the top wall's box also reaches past
both corners, so that no gap remains there.

The wall triangles are added as they are listed in [the chamber data](model.qmd#the-chamber-geometry),
with one correction: Rapier needs their vertices in counter-clockwise order, and lets cells pass
straight through a clockwise triangle. The left and top triangles are listed clockwise (Box2D
reordered them silently), so their vertices are swapped when the sign of the cross product shows
it.

Like the cells' friction (below), the walls' friction is stored as a square root and combined by
multiplication.

```{.typescript #sim-create-walls}
private createWalls(): void {
  const walls = this.world.createRigidBody(RAPIER.RigidBodyDesc.fixed());
  const add = (desc: ColliderDesc) => this.world.createCollider(desc
    .setFriction(Math.sqrt(CHAMBER.friction))
    .setFrictionCombineRule(RAPIER.CoefficientCombineRule.Multiply)
    .setRestitutionCombineRule(RAPIER.CoefficientCombineRule.Max), walls);
  for (const [v1, v2] of CHAMBER.edges) {
    const cx = (v1.x + v2.x) / 2, cy = (v1.y + v2.y) / 2;
    const hx = Math.abs(v1.x - v2.x) / 2, hy = Math.abs(v1.y - v2.y) / 2;
    const t = WALL_THICKNESS / 2;
    if (hx === 0) {
      add(RAPIER.ColliderDesc.cuboid(t, hy).setTranslation(cx + Math.sign(cx) * t, cy));
    } else {
      add(RAPIER.ColliderDesc.cuboid(hx + 2 * t, t).setTranslation(cx, cy + t));
    }
  }
  for (const tri of CHAMBER.triangles) {
    const [a, b, c] = tri.vertices.map((v) => ({ x: v.x + tri.offset.x, y: v.y + tri.offset.y }));
    const clockwise = (b.x - a.x) * (c.y - a.y) - (c.x - a.x) * (b.y - a.y) < 0;
    add(clockwise ? RAPIER.ColliderDesc.triangle(a, c, b) : RAPIER.ColliderDesc.triangle(a, b, c));
  }
}
```

## Cells

### Creating a cell

A new cell draws two random numbers, in the testbed's order: its friction coefficient and its
reproductive length. Its mass and moment of inertia come from the
[Box2D formulas](model.qmd#mass-and-moment-of-inertia) and are set directly on the body (the
collider gets density 0, so that Rapier does not add mass of its own). Bodies never sleep: a
resting cell must still notice when its neighbours grow.

**Friction.** Box2D combines the friction coefficients of two touching shapes as the geometric
mean, $\sqrt{f_1 f_2}$. Rapier has no such rule, but it can multiply. So each collider stores
$\sqrt{f}$, and the *Multiply* rule gives $\sqrt{f_1}\sqrt{f_2} = \sqrt{f_1 f_2}$, exactly Box2D's
value.

Each new cell gets the next id, and its parent is recorded in the lineage (0 for the initial
cells).

```{.typescript #sim-create-cell}
private createCell(x: number, y: number, angle: number, length: number, color: RGB, parentId: number, phase: number): Cell {
  const p = this.params;
  const friction = this.rng();
  const reproductiveLength = p.reproductiveLengthMean + (this.rng() - 0.5) * p.reproductiveLengthSpread;
  const { mass, inertia } = cellMassProperties(length, p.radius, p.density);
  const body = this.world.createRigidBody(RAPIER.RigidBodyDesc.dynamic()
    .setTranslation(x, y)
    .setRotation(angle)
    .setCanSleep(false)
    .setLinearDamping(this.linearDamping(mass))
    .setAngularDamping(this.angularDamping(inertia))
    .setAdditionalMassProperties(mass, this.zero, inertia));
  const sqrtFriction = Math.sqrt(friction);
  const collider = this.world.createCollider(this.cellColliderDesc(length, sqrtFriction), body);
  const id = this.nextId++;
  this.states.addLineage(id, parentId);
  return {
    id, body, collider, sqrtFriction, flipped: false, mass, inertia, length, color, reproductiveLength,
    growthRate: 1 + p.rate, phase, anchors: [], removed: false,
  };
}
```

The collider is a capsule along the body's local $y$ axis, with half-height $\ell/2$ (the distance
from the centre to each end cap's centre) and the cell's radius. Restitution is 0, and combined with
the *Max* rule, as in Box2D.

```{.typescript #sim-collider-desc}
private cellColliderDesc(length: number, sqrtFriction: number): ColliderDesc {
  const p = this.params;
  return RAPIER.ColliderDesc.capsule(length / 2, p.radius)
    .setDensity(0)
    .setFriction(sqrtFriction)
    .setFrictionCombineRule(RAPIER.CoefficientCombineRule.Multiply)
    .setRestitution(p.restitution)
    .setRestitutionCombineRule(RAPIER.CoefficientCombineRule.Max);
}
```

### Drag as damping

With continuous drag, a cell's drag is its body's linear and angular damping, at the
[rates derived in the model](model.qmd#drag-formulas). With the testbed's kick instead
(`continuousDrag` = 0), the bodies get no damping, and the kick is applied on growth steps.

```{.typescript #sim-damping}
private linearDamping(mass: number): number {
  const p = this.params;
  return p.continuousDrag !== 0 ? continuousDampingRate(p.airResistance, mass, p.growthInterval) : 0;
}

private angularDamping(inertia: number): number {
  const p = this.params;
  return p.continuousDrag !== 0 ? continuousDampingRate(p.angularAirResistance, inertia, p.growthInterval) : 0;
}
```

## Growth, division and removal

`growDivideAndMark` handles the cells of one growth group: it grows them, divides those that are
long enough, marks those that left the chamber or died, and updates the cells in the wall zones. It
returns whether any cell was marked for removal.

Cells are only *marked* here and removed afterwards, so that the array is not modified while it is
being walked. Daughters are appended to the end of the array; the loop stops at the length the
array had when it started, so a newborn cell is first handled on its group's next turn.

```{.typescript #sim-grow-divide-mark}
private growDivideAndMark(phase: number): boolean {
  const p = this.params;
  const dt = 1 / p.hertz;
  const kick = p.continuousDrag === 0;
  let marked = false;
  const count = this.cells.length;
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const cell = this.cells[i];
    if (cell.phase !== phase) { continue; }
    const body = cell.body;

    <<sim-grow>>

    <<sim-drag-kick>>

    <<sim-divide>>

    <<sim-leave-or-die>>

    <<sim-wall-zone>>
  }
  return marked;
}
```

### Growth

A cell grows along its long axis by its growth rate, and its collider is replaced or resized to
match ([Growing a collider](#growing-a-collider) explains why this is less simple than it sounds).

```{.typescript #sim-grow}
cell.length *= cell.growthRate;
this.resizeCollider(cell);
```

### The drag kick

Only with `continuousDrag` = 0: the testbed's drag. Box2D applied the force $-k v$ once per fixture
and let it act during the next step; here the same change of velocity is applied at once, as an
impulse $-f\,m\,v$ (and $-f\,I\,\omega$ for the spin), with the fraction $f$ from
[`dragFraction`](model.qmd#drag-formulas).

```{.typescript #sim-drag-kick}
if (kick) {
  const v = body.linvel();
  const linear = -dragFraction(p.airResistance, cell.mass, dt, p.dragClamp !== 0) * cell.mass;
  body.applyImpulse({ x: linear * v.x, y: linear * v.y }, true);
  body.applyTorqueImpulse(-dragFraction(p.angularAirResistance, cell.inertia, dt, p.dragClamp !== 0) * cell.inertia * body.angvel(), true);
}
```

### Division

A cell that has reached its reproductive length divides into two daughters lying along the
parent's axis. Of the parent's straight middle section, $\ell - 2a$, a share $p$ goes to daughter A
and $1-p$ to daughter B:

$$
\ell_A = (\ell - 2a)\,p, \qquad \ell_B = (\ell - 2a)(1 - p).
$$

Their tip-to-tip lengths, $\ell_A + 2a$ and $\ell_B + 2a$, add up to the parent's $\ell + 2a$.
With centred division each daughter sits flush with one end of the parent, so its centre is at a
distance $\ell/2 - \ell_A/2$ (or $\ell/2 - \ell_B/2$) from the parent's centre. The testbed's
placement, kept for `centredDivision` = 0, is slightly off, which made one daughter overlap the
parent's neighbour.

The long axis points along $(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$. The daughter of length $\ell_A$ goes
backwards along it and the daughter of length $\ell_B$ forwards. The first daughter takes over the
parent's body and collider, with a new id and the state of a newborn cell; the second is a new
body. Anchors holding the parent let go, since the parent no longer exists.

```{.typescript #sim-divide}
const length = cell.length;
const position = body.translation();
const angle = body.rotation();
let divided = false;

if (length >= cell.reproductiveLength) {
  const a = p.radius;
  const proportion = p.reproductionProportionMin + this.rng() * p.reproductionProportionRange;
  const lengthA = (length - (2 * a)) * proportion;
  const lengthB = (length - (2 * a)) * (1 - proportion);
  const factorA = p.centredDivision ? length / 2 - lengthB / 2 : proportion * (1 / 2) * length + (a / 2);
  const factorB = p.centredDivision ? length / 2 - lengthA / 2 : (1 - proportion) * (1 / 2) * length + (a / 2);
  const sin = Math.sin(angle), cos = Math.cos(angle);
  const x1 = position.x + factorB * sin, y1 = position.y - factorB * cos;
  const x2 = position.x - factorA * sin, y2 = position.y + factorA * cos;

  const color = cell.color;
  const parentId = cell.id;
  this.detachAnchors(cell, true);
  this.resetCell(cell, x1, y1, angle, lengthA, color, parentId);
  this.cells.push(this.createCell(x2, y2, angle, lengthB, color, parentId, cell.phase));
  divided = true;
}
```

Reusing the parent's body for the first daughter saves creating and destroying a body at every
division. `resetCell` turns it into a newborn cell: it draws the same two random numbers as
`createCell`, in the same order, moves and stops the body, gives it the new mass, damping and
friction, and refreshes its collider.

```{.typescript #sim-reset-cell}
private resetCell(cell: Cell, x: number, y: number, angle: number, length: number, color: RGB, parentId: number): void {
  const p = this.params;
  const friction = this.rng();
  cell.reproductiveLength = p.reproductiveLengthMean + (this.rng() - 0.5) * p.reproductiveLengthSpread;
  const { mass, inertia } = cellMassProperties(length, p.radius, p.density);
  const body = cell.body;
  body.setTranslation({ x, y }, true);
  body.setRotation(angle, true);
  body.setLinvel(this.zero, true);
  body.setAngvel(0, true);
  body.setAdditionalMassProperties(mass, this.zero, inertia, true);
  if (p.continuousDrag !== 0) {
    body.setLinearDamping(this.linearDamping(mass));
    body.setAngularDamping(this.angularDamping(inertia));
  }
  cell.mass = mass;
  cell.inertia = inertia;
  cell.length = length;
  cell.sqrtFriction = Math.sqrt(friction);
  cell.collider.setFriction(cell.sqrtFriction);
  this.resizeCollider(cell);
  cell.color = color;
  cell.growthRate = 1 + p.rate;
  cell.id = this.nextId++;
  this.states.addLineage(cell.id, parentId);
}
```

### Leaving the chamber, and death

A cell whose centre is outside the chamber's box leaves the simulation. A cell inside dies with a
small probability. The `||` matters for reproducibility: the random number for death is drawn only
when the cell is inside, exactly as in the testbed, so the sequence of random numbers, and hence
the run, stays the same. All checks use the position before division; if the cell divided, its
daughters stay even when the parent would have left or died.

```{.typescript #sim-leave-or-die}
if (position.x < p.minX || position.x > p.maxX || position.y < p.minY || position.y > p.maxY || this.rng() < p.randomDeathProbability) {
  if (!divided) { cell.removed = true; marked = true; }
}
```

### Near the walls

A cell within `wallZone` of a side wall turns green and grows at `wallRate`, and may attach to the
surface. Elsewhere it turns magenta and grows at `rate`. A cell that just divided is left alone:
`resetCell` has given the first daughter its parent's colour and the default growth rate, and both
daughters are updated on their group's next turn.

The anchor reproduces another testbed quirk: a cell that divided or was marked for removal in this
same pass still draws its random number and may create an anchor, but the anchor holds nothing.

```{.typescript #sim-wall-zone}
if (position.x < p.minX + p.wallZone || position.x > p.maxX - p.wallZone) {
  if (!divided) {
    cell.color = COLOR_WALL;
    cell.growthRate = 1 + p.wallRate;
  }
  if (this.rng() < p.anchorProbability) {
    this.createAnchor(position.x, position.y, divided || cell.removed ? null : cell);
  }
} else if (!divided) {
  cell.color = COLOR_CENTRE;
  cell.growthRate = 1 + p.rate;
}
```

### Removing cells

Marked cells are removed in one pass that compacts the array in place. Removing a body also
removes its springs, so the anchors only need to forget the cell.

```{.typescript #sim-remove-marked-cells}
private removeMarkedCells(): void {
  let kept = 0;
  for (const cell of this.cells) {
    if (cell.removed) {
      this.detachAnchors(cell, false);
      this.world.removeRigidBody(cell.body);
    } else {
      this.cells[kept++] = cell;
    }
  }
  this.cells.length = kept;
}
```

## Growing a collider

Growing a cell should be as simple as making its capsule longer, and Rapier offers
`setHalfHeight` for exactly that. It does not work here, because of how Rapier (version 0.21)
caches contacts. When two colliders barely move relative to each other, Rapier keeps their contact
points from the previous step, and changing a collider's shape does not refresh them. A cell at
rest, as most cells are once the chamber is full, then grows straight into its neighbours and into
the walls while the contact keeps reporting zero depth. Overlaps rose steadily as the chamber
filled. `tools/rapier-stale-contacts.mjs` reproduces the bug in a few lines.

`refreshContacts` chooses the remedy:

- **1 (default): replace the collider.** A new collider gets fresh contacts. Rapier leaks some
  WebAssembly memory for every replaced collider that touches others, though: about 13 MB per 1000
  steps with a full chamber, enough to exhaust the 4 GB WebAssembly heap after about 230 000 steps.
  Freeing a whole world returns the memory, so the simulation [rebuilds the world](#rebuilding-the-world)
  every `rebuildInterval` steps.
- **2: resize in place, then turn the collider by π.** The capsule is symmetric, so it occupies the
  same space, but the turn makes Rapier recompute most of its contacts, without allocating.
  Contacts between two cells that both turned are sometimes missed, and overlaps were worse.
- **0: resize in place only**, with stale contacts, to show the effect.

```{.typescript #sim-resize-collider}
private resizeCollider(cell: Cell): void {
  switch (this.params.refreshContacts) {
    case 1:
      this.world.removeCollider(cell.collider, false);
      cell.collider = this.world.createCollider(this.cellColliderDesc(cell.length, cell.sqrtFriction), cell.body);
      break;
    case 2:
      cell.collider.setHalfHeight(cell.length / 2);
      cell.flipped = !cell.flipped;
      cell.collider.setRotationWrtParent(cell.flipped ? Math.PI : 0);
      break;
    default:
      cell.collider.setHalfHeight(cell.length / 2);
  }
}
```

### Rebuilding the world

A rebuild moves everything into a fresh world and frees the old one. Every cell gets a new body
with exactly its old position, angle, velocities, mass and damping, and a new collider; the walls
and the anchors' fixed bodies and springs are recreated. Contacts start fresh, just as they do
after any collider replacement, so the simulation carries on as if nothing had happened, and the
memory Rapier leaked is returned.

```{.typescript #sim-rebuild-world}
private rebuildWorld(): void {
  const old = this.world;
  this.world = this.createWorld();
  for (const cell of this.cells) {
    const t = cell.body.translation(), v = cell.body.linvel();
    const body = this.world.createRigidBody(RAPIER.RigidBodyDesc.dynamic()
      .setTranslation(t.x, t.y)
      .setRotation(cell.body.rotation())
      .setLinvel(v.x, v.y)
      .setAngvel(cell.body.angvel())
      .setCanSleep(false)
      .setLinearDamping(this.linearDamping(cell.mass))
      .setAngularDamping(this.angularDamping(cell.inertia))
      .setAdditionalMassProperties(cell.mass, this.zero, cell.inertia));
    cell.body = body;
    cell.collider = this.world.createCollider(this.cellColliderDesc(cell.length, cell.sqrtFriction)
      .setRotation(cell.flipped ? Math.PI : 0), body);
  }
  this.createWalls();
  for (const anchor of this.anchors) {
    anchor.body = this.world.createRigidBody(RAPIER.RigidBodyDesc.fixed().setTranslation(anchor.x, anchor.y));
    if (anchor.cell) {
      const data = RAPIER.JointData.spring(0, anchor.stiffness, anchor.damping, this.zero, this.zero);
      anchor.joint = this.world.createImpulseJoint(data, anchor.cell.body, anchor.body, true);
    }
  }
  old.free();
}
```

## Anchors

An anchor is a fixed body at the attachment point and a spring of rest length zero between it and
the cell's centre. The spring constants are Box2D's for a body held by a static one: for a cell of
mass $m$, natural frequency $\nu$ (`anchorFrequencyHz`) and damping ratio $\zeta$,

$$
\omega = 2\pi\nu, \qquad k = m\,\omega^2, \qquad c = 2\,m\,\zeta\,\omega .
$$

Rapier's spring joint applies these as forces; with $\nu = 0.8$ Hz a held cell swings with a period
of 1.25 s. An anchor created without a cell (see [Near the walls](#near-the-walls)) is just a fixed
point.

```{.typescript #sim-create-anchor}
private createAnchor(x: number, y: number, cell: Cell | null): void {
  const p = this.params;
  const body = this.world.createRigidBody(RAPIER.RigidBodyDesc.fixed().setTranslation(x, y));
  const anchor: Anchor = { body, x, y, createdAtStep: this.stepCount, cell, joint: null, stiffness: 0, damping: 0 };
  if (cell) {
    const mass = cell.body.mass();
    const omega = 2 * Math.PI * p.anchorFrequencyHz;
    anchor.stiffness = mass * omega * omega;
    anchor.damping = 2 * mass * p.anchorDampingRatio * omega;
    const data = RAPIER.JointData.spring(0, anchor.stiffness, anchor.damping, this.zero, this.zero);
    anchor.joint = this.world.createImpulseJoint(data, cell.body, body, true);
    cell.anchors.push(anchor);
  }
  this.anchors.push(anchor);
}
```

When a cell divides or is removed, its anchors stop holding it. On division the springs are removed
explicitly; on removal there is no need, since removing the cell's body removes its springs too.

```{.typescript #sim-detach-anchors}
private detachAnchors(cell: Cell, removeJoints: boolean): void {
  for (const anchor of cell.anchors) {
    if (removeJoints && anchor.joint) { this.world.removeImpulseJoint(anchor.joint, true); }
    anchor.joint = null;
    anchor.cell = null;
  }
  cell.anchors.length = 0;
}
```

Once per growth cycle, anchors that have expired, or whose cell has been dragged more than
`anchorMaxStretch` away, are removed. Removing an anchor's fixed body removes its spring.

```{.typescript #sim-remove-anchors}
private removeAnchors(): void {
  const p = this.params;
  let kept = 0;
  for (const anchor of this.anchors) {
    if (this.stepCount - anchor.createdAtStep >= p.anchorLifetimeSteps || this.overStretched(anchor)) {
      if (anchor.cell) { anchor.cell.anchors.splice(anchor.cell.anchors.indexOf(anchor), 1); }
      this.world.removeRigidBody(anchor.body);
    } else {
      this.anchors[kept++] = anchor;
    }
  }
  this.anchors.length = kept;
}
```

```{.typescript #sim-over-stretched}
private overStretched(anchor: Anchor): boolean {
  const max = this.params.anchorMaxStretch;
  if (max <= 0 || !anchor.cell) { return false; }
  const t = anchor.cell.body.translation();
  return Math.hypot(t.x - anchor.x, t.y - anchor.y) > max;
}
```

## Snapshots

A snapshot records every cell's centre, id, orientation and length at full precision; the
[recorder](recording.qmd#recording-states) rounds and stores them.

```{.typescript #sim-take-snapshot}
private takeSnapshot(): void {
  const cells: CellState[] = [];
  for (const cell of this.cells) {
    const t = cell.body.translation();
    cells.push({ x: t.x, y: t.y, id: cell.id, an: orientationOf(cell.body.rotation()), le: cell.length });
  }
  this.states.addSnapshot(cells);
}
```
